Transistor Operating Regions: Cutoff, Active and Saturation With Load Line, Relay Driver Example and Calculator

A BJT sits in cutoff, active or saturation, and the bias on its two junctions decides which. Learn to read the region from VBE and VCE, then use that to design a relay driver that switches cleanly.

Cutoff Active Saturation Load Line Relay Driver

How a BJT moves between cutoff, active and saturation, and how to find the region from two meter readings. We work through a 2N3904 relay driver with a load line chart and a calculator.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn transistor operating regions with a real relay driver, a load line and simple field measurements.
Quick Answer

What are transistor operating regions in a BJT?

Transistor operating regions are the bias states of a BJT: cutoff (both junctions off, IC almost zero), active (base emitter forward, base collector reverse, IC = β × IB) and saturation (both junctions forward, VCE about 0.2 V). Example: with VCC = 12 V and a 400 Ω relay coil, an IB of 1.95 mA forces saturation because β × IB of 117 mA is far above the 29.5 mA the coil allows.

What Are Transistor Operating Regions?

The transistor operating regions are cutoff, active and saturation, and the bias of the base emitter and base collector junctions decides which one a BJT is in. Switching circuits live in cutoff and saturation, while amplifiers keep the transistor in the active region around a fixed Q point.

Key Facts
  • Cutoff: VBE below about 0.5 V, IC is only nanoamp leakage, VCE equals the supply.
  • Active: VBE about 0.6 to 0.7 V, base collector reverse biased, IC = β × IB.
  • Saturation: both junctions forward biased, VCE(sat) about 0.1 to 0.3 V for small signal silicon parts.

If base, collector and emitter are new to you, start with our basics of transistors. The table gives the junction bias for an NPN part, and on a PNP part every polarity flips.

RegionBase emitter junctionBase collector junctionTypical VCECollector currentUsed for
CutoffReverse or below 0.5 VReverseAbout VCCLeakage only, nASwitch OFF
Active (forward active)Forward, about 0.65 VReverseAbove about 0.3 VIC = β × IBAmplifier, current source
SaturationForward, 0.7 to 0.85 VForward0.1 to 0.3 VSet by VCC and RCSwitch ON
Reverse activeReverseForwardSmall, emitter acts as collectorVery low gainRarely used, some TTL inputs
Do You Know?

Saturation means opposite things in a BJT and a MOSFET. Toshiba points out that in a BJT it is the end of current amplification, while in a MOSFET the saturation region is the flat part of the curve where the device can amplify.

How Does a BJT Move Between Cutoff, Active and Saturation?

Base current decides which of the transistor operating regions a BJT sits in: zero base current means cutoff, a moderate base current means active, and more base current than the load can use means saturation. The ceiling is set by the supply and load, because IC can never exceed (VCC minus VCE(sat)) divided by RC.

Cutoff

VBE stays below the knee, so almost no electrons enter the base. The 2N3904 datasheet allows only 50 nA of collector cutoff current at 30 V.

Best for: Switch OFF state
OFF
Active

Electrons from the emitter cross the thin base and are swept into the reverse biased collector, so IC follows β × IB.

Best for: Amplifiers and current sources
LINEAR
Saturation

Extra base drive forward biases the collector junction too. VCE collapses and IC is set by the external circuit, not by β.

Best for: Relay, lamp and solenoid switching
ON

Toshiba explains why: once the collector junction is forward biased, the electron gradient across the base flattens and more electrons recombine there, so extra base current no longer raises collector current. That is why the apparent hFE in saturation is far below the active gain on the datasheet.

Apply Kirchhoff's voltage law around the collector loop and you get VCC = IC × RC + VCE in all transistor operating regions. Our article on BJT currents and voltages derives IE = IB + IC, which also holds everywhere.

Quick Tip

One check sorts the three regions, and it is the collector junction. If the base is driven and that junction is still reverse biased, the BJT is active; if both junctions conduct, it is saturated; if neither conducts, it is in cutoff.

Transistor as a Switch vs Amplifier: Which Region Do You Need?

A transistor used as a switch must jump between cutoff and saturation, while an amplifier must stay inside the active region for the whole signal swing.

The circuit above is the standard low side relay driver found on PLC interface boards and microcontroller cards. It works the same way as the sinking outputs described in sinking and sourcing in PLC, where an NPN stage pulls the load to 0 V.

Switch mode (cutoff and saturation)
  • Very low power loss in both states because either IC or VCE is close to zero.
  • Design with minimum β and an overdrive of 2 to 10 times.
  • Saturation adds storage time, 200 ns max for a 2N3904 at 10 mA.
Amplifier mode (active region)
  • Q point placed near the middle of the load line for maximum swing.
  • Design for stable IC against β spread using emitter resistor bias.
  • Dissipation is highest here, up to VCC² ÷ 4RC at mid supply.
Saturation design rule:
IC(sat) = (VCC minus VCE(sat)) ÷ RC
IB(min) = IC(sat) ÷ β(min)
IB(design) = 2 to 10 × IB(min)
RB = (VIN minus VBE) ÷ IB(design)

Transistor Operating Regions Solved Example: 2N3904 Relay Driver

With VCC = 12 V, a 400 Ω coil, RB = 2.2 kΩ, a 5 V input and β(min) = 60, the transistor saturates with an overdrive of about 4. The working below uses the same defaults as the calculator.

IB = (5 minus 0.7) ÷ 2.2 kΩ = 1.955 mA
IC(sat) = (12 minus 0.2) ÷ 400 Ω = 29.50 mA
β × IB = 60 × 1.955 mA = 117.3 mA
117.3 mA is more than 29.50 mA, so
Region = saturation, VCE = 0.2 V
Overdrive = 117.3 ÷ 29.50 = 3.98

We took β = 60 because the onsemi datasheet guarantees hFE of only 60 minimum at 50 mA and 100 minimum at 10 mA, and a switch must work with the worst part in the box. Now change RB to 100 kΩ: IB drops to 43 µA, β × IB is only 2.58 mA, and VCE = 12 minus (2.58 mA × 400 Ω) = 10.97 V.

In that second case the coil sees about 1 V instead of 11.8 V, so the relay never clicks. Where the curve for your IB meets the orange load line is the operating point, so you can read all three transistor operating regions straight off this chart.

Transistor Operating Regions Calculator (NPN, silicon)
Result (VBE 0.7 V and VCE(sat) 0.2 V assumed)
Saturation region: IB = 1.955 mA, IC = 29.50 mA, VCE = 0.20 V, overdrive 3.98

The calculator uses Ohm's law on the base and collector loops and compares β × IB with IC(sat). Keep the overdrive above 2 for relays and take the coil resistance from the relay datasheet.

How to Check if a Transistor Is in Saturation or Active Region?

Measure VBE and VCE with a multimeter while the input is held steady: VCE below about 0.3 V with VBE near 0.7 V means saturation, VCE well above 0.3 V with VBE near 0.65 V means active, and VBE below 0.5 V means cutoff. These two readings identify transistor operating regions on any working silicon BJT.

Measured VBEMeasured VCERegionWhat it tells you
0 to 0.4 VAbout VCCCutoffNo base drive, or input LOW
0.6 to 0.7 V0.5 V up to near VCCActiveBase drive present but not enough for the load
0.7 to 0.85 V0.05 to 0.3 VSaturationSwitch fully ON
Above 1 V with input HIGHAbout VCCFaultBase emitter junction likely open

Measure from the emitter, not a distant ground, because a few hundred millivolts of ground drop can make a saturated transistor look active.

1
Hold the input
Force the control input HIGH with the PLC or a test jumper.
2
Read VBE
Black probe on the emitter, red on the base; expect 0.7 to 0.85 V for a driven switch.
3
Read VCE
Move the red probe to the collector; a healthy switch reads 0.3 V or less.
4
Repeat with input LOW
VBE should fall to near 0 V and VCE should rise to VCC.
Do You Know?

A saturated BJT does not turn off instantly. The 2N3904 datasheet specifies a storage time of up to 200 ns, which is the time the extra charge in the base takes to clear before the collector current starts to fall.

Transistor Relay Driver Not Switching: Troubleshooting Flowchart

If a relay does not pull in, the transistor is usually in cutoff because drive is missing, or stuck in the active region because the base current is too small for the coil. The flowchart sorts the fault using transistor operating regions and only two readings, VBE and VCE.

One field cause is a coil swapped for a lower resistance type, which raises IC(sat) while the old RB still delivers the same base current. A second cause is a missing coil suppression diode, because the inductive kick at turn off can break down the collector junction and leave the transistor shorted.

  • Input HIGH level reaches the base resistor (check the PLC or logic output first).
  • VBE between 0.7 and 0.85 V when ON.
  • VCE at or below 0.3 V when ON.
  • Flyback diode fitted with its cathode on the supply side.
  • Overdrive of at least 2 using minimum datasheet β.
Myth: More base current always gives more collector current.
Fact: Only in the active region; in saturation IC is fixed by VCC and the load, and extra base current only adds storage time.
Myth: A transistor in saturation is overloaded or damaged.
Fact: Saturation is the normal ON state of a switch, and it is where dissipation is lowest.
Myth: VCE of 1 V means the transistor is ON.
Fact: With a 2N3904 at tens of milliamps, 1 V is the active region and wastes power; a good switch reads 0.3 V or less.

Where Do Transistor Operating Regions Matter in Instrumentation?

You meet the switching regions in output drivers and the active region in signal conditioning, so transistor operating regions explain both a PLC output card and a sensor amplifier.

PLC and DCS output cards
NPN or PNP stages drive relays, solenoid valves and indicator lamps in cutoff and saturation.
Proximity sensor outputs
Inductive and capacitive sensors switch their NPN or PNP output transistor hard ON and OFF.
Optocoupler outputs
The output phototransistor must saturate to give a clean logic level.

For the active region in practice, see the common emitter amplifier article, and for sensor wiring read NPN and PNP proximity sensors. The output stage of an optocoupler follows the same rules, except that the base current comes from light.

A Darlington pair gives huge gain, but its output VCE cannot fall below the VCE(sat) of the driver plus one VBE. When that drop matters, a logic level MOSFET is often the better switch.

Quick Tip

If a switching transistor runs warm, measure VCE first. A switch sitting at 2 to 5 V is in the active region, and that is where the power goes.

When a driver must dissipate real power, run the numbers through our heat sink calculator. For the 12 V, 400 Ω example, the worst case active point at VCE = 6 V dissipates 90 mW, while the saturated switch dissipates only about 6 mW.

Transistor Operating Regions FAQ

What is the difference between active and saturation region in a BJT?

In the active region the base collector junction is reverse biased and IC equals β times IB. In saturation both junctions are forward biased, VCE drops to about 0.2 V and IC is limited by VCC and the load.

Among transistor operating regions, amplifiers use the first and switches use the second.

How do you calculate whether a transistor is in saturation step by step?

Find IB = (VIN minus 0.7) ÷ RB and IC(sat) = (VCC minus 0.2) ÷ RC. If β × IB is larger than IC(sat), the transistor saturates.

With 12 V, 400 Ω, 2.2 kΩ and β = 60, β × IB is 117 mA against 29.5 mA, so it saturates.

What VCE value tells you a transistor is fully switched on?

For small signal silicon transistors a VCE of 0.3 V or less means saturation. The 2N3904 datasheet guarantees 0.2 V max at 10 mA with 1 mA base current.

Readings near 1 V or higher mean the part is still in the active region.

Why should a transistor switch be designed with forced beta of 10?

A forced beta of about 10 gives several times the base current needed even with the lowest datasheet gain. That margin covers hFE spread, temperature and coil tolerance.

Datasheets also specify VCE(sat) at IC ÷ IB = 10, so the guaranteed value applies.

Why does my transistor relay driver get hot and not click?

The transistor is stuck in the active region because the base current is too small for the coil current. Part of the supply then drops across the transistor as heat.

Reduce RB, check that the input really reaches the base, or use a MOSFET driver.

What We Learn Today

  • Transistor operating regions are set by junction bias: cutoff with both junctions off, active with only the base emitter on, and saturation with both on.
  • A switch needs IB at least two to ten times IC(sat) divided by minimum beta, so VCE falls to about 0.2 V and dissipation stays low.
  • Two meter readings, VBE and VCE taken from the emitter, are enough to locate the operating point and troubleshoot a relay driver that refuses to switch.
